Broad whitefish (Coregonus nasus) embryos experience a prolonged period of yolk-dependent development following egg fertilisation, with hatching occurring after the chorion is ruptured by chorionase secretion. The larval eclosion from the demersal egg gives rise to a yolk-sac larva that remains endotrophic until mouth opening enables first exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth for newly emerged prolarvae has been estimated at 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams], a value derived from egg diameter measurements of related coregonines and reflecting the modest energy reserves available to the lecithotrophic larva before it must commence active prey capture. This relatively small birth mass is typical for cold-water salmonids that produce numerous small offspring, a reproductive strategy that trades individual offspring size for greater fecundity. During the early larval phase, these free-swimming ichthyoplankton drift with currents in pelagic zones, gradually depleting their yolk reserves as they develop the sensory and locomotor capabilities needed for the trophic switch to exogenous feeding.

Sexual maturation in Broad whitefish is a gradual process influenced by the cold thermal regime of Arctic and subarctic waters, with puberty attained at a total length that has been well characterised from field studies. Individuals reach the stage of reproductive activation when they achieve a body length of 35 cm [Lp = 35 cm], a size that corresponds to the estimated wet weight at puberty of 475 grams [Wwp = 475 grams] based on empirical length-weight relationships developed for this species. The transition to a reproductively viable adult does not occur until fish have accumulated sufficient somatic energy reserves over several growing seasons, a constraint that is particularly stringent in high-latitude populations where the growing season is brief. Young-of-the-year and juvenile fish grow slowly during their first summers, and it is not uncommon for sub-adults to require between five and nine years of age before reaching the threshold length for first spawning. This delayed onset of reproductive activity is a common life-history pattern among coregonines inhabiting nutrient-poor, cold environments.

Spawning adults of Broad whitefish migrate from lake feeding areas into tributary streams during the autumn, where gravid individuals broadcast spawn over gravel substrates at temperatures around 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate translates into an annual output of approximately 384 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 384 eggs per year]. This reproductive strategy, which yields a moderate number of relatively large demersal eggs, contrasts with the high fecundity observed in many marine teleosts but is consistent with the need for offspring to survive long, cold winters with limited food availability. The yolky, adhesive eggs are deposited in interstitial spaces of the gravel, where they incubate slowly throughout the winter months.

As Broad whitefish continue to grow and accumulate mass across their adult years, they eventually approach an asymptotic maximum size that is rarely surpassed even in the most productive habitats. Application of a length-weight allometric equation to the observed adult length of approximately 71 cm [Li = approximately 71 cm] yields an estimated asymptotic adult wet mass of roughly 4600 grams [Wwi = roughly 4600 grams] in Broad whitefish populations from productive Arctic deltas. This substantial body mass, achieved only after many years of feeding in productive delta and lake ecosystems, places Coregonus nasus among the larger members of its genus. The growth trajectory in these fish is characterised by a rapid juvenile phase followed by a pronounced deceleration after the onset of reproductive activity, as energy that might otherwise fuel structural growth is increasingly diverted toward gamete production and spawning migrations. Comparisons with other coregonines, such as Coregonus lavaretus and Coregonus clupeaformis, reveal that Broad whitefish attains a comparable or slightly larger adult size under similar environmental conditions.

The lifespan of Broad whitefish is notably extended for a relatively fast-growing salmonid, with the oldest documented individuals persisting for up to 15 years [am = up to 15 years] when maintained in habitats where thermal conditions average 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This longevity reflects the species' adaptation to cold, stable environments where metabolic rates are low and the accumulation of oxidative damage is slowed, allowing senescent adult death to occur much later than in temperate or tropical teleosts of equivalent body size. Natural mortality in older cohorts is often linked to the energetic exhaustion associated with repeated spawning migrations rather than to acute predation or disease, as the large body size of spawning adults provides some refuge from most aquatic predators. Field records indicate that post-reproductive mortality becomes increasingly common after the age of twelve years, with very few individuals surviving beyond the fifteenth winter. This life history, combining slow juvenile growth, delayed puberty, modest annual reproductive output, and a long adult lifespan, positions Broad whitefish as a classic cold-water strategist within the subfamily Coregoninae.
